units: a depot supervisor lays out two routes for a newly hired driver
the expressway has a recent safety barrier and a toll point where you get on
the surface of the expressway is smooth and barely shakes the vehicle
the second route runs through small towns whose pavement has broken open
speed humps rise before the intersections of the second route
the driver objects to the direct run on grounds of cost and boredom
the supervisor holds that a broken road wears the mechanics more than the toll costs
the driver comes around to her supervisor and picks the expressway
text: The depot supervisor laid out both routes for the newly hired driver and told her straight off that they were not equal. The first runs along an expressway with a fresh safety barrier the whole way and a toll point where you get on. The surface there stays smooth, so the cab barely shudders. The other cuts through small towns where the pavement has broken open into holes, and a speed hump rises before every intersection. She pushed back: the direct run costs money, and the sameness of it wears you down. Her supervisor answered that torn-up pavement chews through suspension far faster than any toll eats into the day's takings. A swerve caused by an unmarked hole, he added, comes dearer still. In the end she granted that safety weighed more than the saving, and she settled on the expressway.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: trade called for surfaces able to carry heavily loaded wagons
the width of the way had to let two teams pass each other
military needs produced straight lines and evenly spaced stopping places
ordinary travelers gained places to rest and points to draw water
carved markers announced the distance still to be covered
upkeep forced itself in because a neglected way breaks down and closes over
these old concerns turn up in the networks still being built
text: Organized road networks grew out of needs that had little to do with one another. Commerce came first. The builders had to lay down a surface firm enough that a loaded wagon would not sink into it, and wide enough that two teams could pass without either one halting. Warfare pushed next, and it pushed differently: straight lines, and stopping places set at even intervals so a column could move without scattering. Only later did anyone think of the ordinary traveler, who gained wayside inns, watering troughs, and carved markers announcing how far was left to go. Upkeep settled the matter on its own, since a way nobody tends will rut, fill with brush, and shrink back to a footpath. Every one of those old concerns turns up again, barely altered, in the networks we are still building today.

units: marks on the ground show where the doors will open
you have to wait for riders to get off before stepping on
two streams meeting in the doorway slow the whole exchange
once aboard it is better to work toward the middle of the car
the entry step turns slick in rain and brings people down
you are advised to get ready to leave one stop before the one you want
forcing the door is a bad idea and you can come back on the other track
text: You step onto the platform, and the first thing to do is spot where the doors will line up. Painted marks on the ground tell you. Then let people off. Sounds obvious, but two streams meeting in the doorway obstruct the whole exchange and cost the entire carriage a solid minute. Once you are aboard, work your way toward the middle instead of stationing yourself beside the entrance. The boarding step deserves some attention when it rains, because the surface turns slick and passengers go down fast. On the way out, get yourself ready one stop early: bag closed, one hand free. And if you miss it, whatever you do, don't wrestle with the door. Ride to the next one, cross over, and come back on the other track. Nothing dramatic happens, unless you insist on fixing your mistake in a rush.

units: a front tire tore open on the edge of a hole in the surface
the steering yanked hard and the coach left its line
the driver gave up on hard braking so as not to unsettle the heavy truck behind him
he let the side barrier take the friction of the vehicle
the riders heard the body grinding along the metal for a long stretch
the inquiry showed that the repair of the surface had been botched
the top layer had peeled loose after a wet season
what the riders take away is that the barrier held
text: A single blown tire was enough to turn a routine run into an emergency. The coach was holding the right lane when the front wheel tore itself open against the edge of a badly patched hole. The steering yanked hard, and the vehicle began veering off toward the shoulder. The driver did not stand on the brake, a maneuver that would have swung the trailer of the truck riding behind him. He eased off the accelerator instead and let the side barrier absorb the friction. The passengers, shaken about, heard the bodywork grinding along the metal for a long stretch before the whole thing came to rest. The investigation established afterward that the surface had been patched in haste after a wet season, and that the top layer had peeled loose. What the riders take away is simpler: the barrier held.

units: loading a luggage bay is a matter of method and not of muscle
the bags arrive in no order while the space available is fixed
you are advised to sort the bags on the ground before opening the hatch
hard cases and soft bags are split into two groups
the heaviest pieces go against the back wall
the soft bags fill the hollows the cases leave
the bags for the first stop go near the opening
a well built load does not shift under braking
text: Loading a luggage bay calls for method rather than muscle, and the trouble comes from one thing only: the bags arrive in whatever order they arrive, while the space forgives nothing. So begin on the ground, unhurried, before you ever swing the hatch open. Set the rigid cases to one side, the collapsible bags to the other, and keep apart whatever will have to come out along the way. Then stand the heaviest pieces against the back wall, flat, edge toward you; they will form a base that does not shift. Push the soft bags into the hollows the cases leave, the way straw is packed into a mattress. Save the space by the opening for what gets off at the first stop. A bay built this way stays motionless under braking, and the unloading runs its course without anything tumbling onto the stones.

units: two ways of collecting tolls work on the same road corridor
the barrier setup forces vehicles to come to a full stop
the queue stretches as soon as traffic thickens at the barrier setup
the repeated pull-aways drive up fuel use among heavy trucks
the overhead reader lets vehicles through without any break in pace
throughput measured at the reader runs well above that of the barriers
the loss of the braking cuts wear on the surface
automatic reading fails when plates are dirty
collecting after the fact brings a heavier load of paperwork
text: Two ways of collecting tolls now operate along the same corridor, and the readings taken at the recently opened interchange show just how far apart they sit. The barrier plaza, with its sorting lanes, forces every vehicle to a full stop. Throughput there hits a ceiling, the queue stretches as soon as traffic thickens, and the repeated pull-aways drive up the fuel consumption of the heavy trucks. The overhead reader mounted on the access ramp lets vehicles through at an unbroken pace. Throughput measured there triples, and wear on the surface drops, since the repeated braking has disappeared. Technicians point to one weakness in exchange: the reader fails on dirty plates, and collection then falls back on billing after the fact, which is considerably more expensive to process. Smoother flow, in short, is bought with paperwork.

units: the moored vessel takes up the whole length of the pier
a row of round openings ringed in brass runs level with the water
the level given over to vehicles looks like a wide metal hall
the access ramps clatter under passing wheels
the cabin floor is known by its narrow passageways and numbered doors
the topmost deck takes the walkers and holds benches bolted down
a lowered gangway joins the stern of the vessel to the pier
two thick lines hold the vessel against the swell
text: The moored vessel takes up the full length of the pier, and its construction reads level by level. Down at the bottom, the dark hull barely breaks the surface of the water, and a row of round portholes runs along it, each one ringed in brass that the salt air has tarnished. Above that opens the vehicle deck, an immense metal cavern where the ramps clatter under passing wheels. Next comes the cabin floor, known at once by its narrow passageways and the numbered doors that follow one another without a break. The topmost deck belongs to walkers: benches bolted down, an unbroken railing, a signal mast, a funnel as broad as a tower. Astern, a lowered gangway reaches the concrete of the pier, and two thick lines, drawn tight on the diagonal, hold the whole vessel steady against the swell.

units: roadways were widened in the name of easy driving
shops were moved out to the edges where parking was plentiful
that move stretched the distances each of us has to cover
doubling the lanes was followed by an even thicker jam
a recent reversal narrows the roadways and hands space back to people on foot and on bicycles
the writer refuses to read that reversal as a passing fashion
the old mistake lay in treating traffic as a fixed volume
traffic in fact answers to the lanes it is offered
text: Before judging the state of our streets, it helps to walk back through the decisions that made them. Roadways were widened first, on the belief that easy driving would serve everyone. Shops were then pushed out to the edges, where parking was plentiful, which stretched the distances each of us has to cover. Jams showed up anyway, so the lanes were doubled, and the jams came back thicker than before. Lately the order has reversed: roadways are narrowing, trees are going in, space is handed back to people on foot and on bicycles. Call it fashion if you like, but fashion is not what it is. It corrects a mistake several generations old, one that treated traffic as a fixed volume of fluid rather than a demand shaped by the lanes offered to it. Worth remembering before the next job starts.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman driving the evening service did not choose this work at the start
she worked as a mechanic in a shop that closed
the closing of the shop pushed her to take the heavy-vehicle license
her time with engines lets her catch a worn suspension at the first speed hump
she calls out faults before they can cut the service short
knowing the frame lets her ease over obstacles gently
she had the entry step replaced because its worn edge troubled older riders
her line logs fewer incidents than the others
the company has handed her the training of incoming drivers
text: The woman who drives the evening service never set out to do this work. She started as a mechanic in a repair shop. The shop closed, and she took the heavy-vehicle license because nothing better came along. Her years with engines ended up serving her well. She feels a worn suspension at the first speed hump, and she calls the fault in before it can strand the line. Knowing the frame by heart, she eases over the humps so gently that her riders no longer bang into the seat in front of them. She also got the entry step replaced, since a worn edge made climbing aboard risky for older passengers. The outcome is plain: her line logs fewer incidents than the others, and the company now hands her the incoming drivers to train. She laughs about it, having only ever wanted to repair motors.

units: the recently opened bus terminal was met with polite praise
the boarding bays run in a line along a single corridor
nothing hung overhead helps the traveler find his coach
a rider in a hurry has to walk the whole row before spotting his departure
the hall throws back an echo and makes spoken announcements impossible to follow
panels hung above each bay would settle the question of direction
absorbent material set under the roof beams would help hearing
the number of benches ought to be doubled
the writer finds the structure sound but its use badly thought out
text: The recently opened bus terminal deserves better than the polite praise that greeted it. Its main flaw hits you at the door: the boarding bays run down a single corridor with nothing hung overhead to mark them, so a rider in a hurry walks the whole row before spotting his coach. The hall, for its part, rings hollow and stretches the announcements until nobody can follow them. All of this would amount to failure if the building gave us nothing to work with. The remedies exist, though, and they come cheap. Lit panels hung above each bay would settle the question of direction. Absorbent material fixed under the roof beams would give the voice back its edges. As for the benches, too few of them, doubling the number would do. The frame is sound. It is the use of it that nobody thought through.
